sections.heading: What is amlodipine used for and how does it work?
sections.body:
Amlodipine is a calcium channel blocker. Doctors use it to treat high blood pressure. The NHS says that if you have high blood pressure, taking amlodipine can help to prevent future heart disease, heart attacks and strokes. It is also used for angina, which is chest pain caused by heart disease. MedlinePlus says it is also used for coronary artery disease, and that it helps to control these conditions but does not cure them. The NHS says it works by blocking calcium from going into the muscles of the heart and blood vessels. Muscles need calcium to contract, so blocking it makes the muscle cells relax and the blood vessels widen.

The NHS says most adults and children over the age of 6 can take amlodipine, but it is not suitable for some people. It can be taken at any time of day, but the NHS suggests keeping to about the same time each day. If side effects bother you, the NHS says a doctor may be able to prescribe a different medicine.

sections.heading: What are the side effects of amlodipine?
sections.body:
The NHS lists the common side effects of amlodipine as swelling in the ankles, feet and legs, headaches, dizziness, sleepiness, a pounding heartbeat (palpitations), flushing, feeling sick, constipation or diarrhoea, and tiredness. For swelling, the NHS suggests raising your legs when you are sitting down.

The NHS says some side effects should ease after a week or so as the body gets used to the medicine, but others can last longer. It also says that if you feel dizzy you should not drive, ride a bike or use tools or machinery until the dizziness passes. The NHS advises speaking to a doctor or pharmacist if side effects bother you or do not go away, and says a doctor may be able to prescribe a different medicine.

sections.heading: Which amlodipine side effects are serious?
sections.body:
Serious side effects are rare, according to the NHS. The NHS lists severe stomach pain, which can be a sign of an inflamed pancreas, and yellowing of the whites of the eyes or skin, which can be a sign of liver problems. The yellowing may be less obvious on brown or black skin.

The NHS says to call 999 if your lips, mouth, throat or tongue suddenly swell, or if you have difficulty breathing, because these can be signs of a serious allergic reaction. The NHS also says to call 999 for chest pain that does not go away after a few minutes, or chest pain that is new or worse in someone who already has angina. In these emergencies the NHS says not to drive yourself to A&E.

sections.heading: Grapefruit, alcohol and simvastatin with amlodipine
sections.body:
The NHS says that large amounts of grapefruit or grapefruit juice can raise the level of amlodipine in your body and make side effects worse. The NHS says alcohol can make the blood-pressure-lowering effect of amlodipine stronger. This can cause sleepiness, dizziness or a headache, so the NHS suggests limiting how much you drink. The NHS says amlodipine tablets and liquid can be taken with or without food. Apart from grapefruit and alcohol, the NHS does not list other foods or drinks to avoid.

Amlodipine can also interact with simvastatin, a statin. The UK Drug Safety Update from the MHRA says amlodipine increases exposure to simvastatin, so the maximum recommended dose of simvastatin is limited when the two medicines are taken together.

sections.heading: Who needs extra care with amlodipine?
sections.body:
The NHS says amlodipine is not suitable for everyone. It says the medicine may not suit people who have had an allergic reaction or serious side effect from amlodipine or a similar medicine before. The same NHS list names low blood pressure, heart failure, a recent heart attack and certain heart valve disease. UK patient leaflets say people with severe low blood pressure should not take it.

In pregnancy, the main NHS amlodipine page says it is not usually recommended because there are similar medicines that are safer, but it may be used if other options have failed. A more detailed NHS page says it is not thought to be harmful to the baby, although the evidence is limited. For breastfeeding, the Specialist Pharmacy Service, an NHS service, says amlodipine passes into breast milk usually in very small amounts and that no side effects have been reported in breastfed infants. One NHS page says it is acceptable if the baby is healthy, while the main page says it is not usually used when breastfeeding.

faqs.a: Yes, swelling in the ankles, feet and legs is one of the common side effects listed by the NHS. For swelling, the NHS suggests raising your legs when you are sitting down. The NHS advises speaking to a doctor or pharmacist if side effects bother you or do not go away, and says a doctor may be able to prescribe a different medicine.

faqs.q: Can I drink alcohol while taking amlodipine?
faqs.a: The NHS says alcohol can make the blood-pressure-lowering effect of amlodipine stronger. This can cause sleepiness, dizziness or a headache. The NHS suggests limiting how much alcohol you drink. If you feel dizzy, the NHS says not to drive, ride a bike or use tools or machinery until it passes.

faqs.q: Is grapefruit a problem with amlodipine?
faqs.a: The NHS says large amounts of grapefruit or grapefruit juice can raise the amount of amlodipine in your body. That can make side effects worse. The NHS also says that if side effects bother you, a doctor may be able to prescribe a different medicine.

faqs.q: Can I take amlodipine if I am pregnant or breastfeeding?
faqs.a: The main NHS amlodipine page says it is not usually recommended in pregnancy because there are similar medicines that are safer, but it may be used if other options have failed. A more detailed NHS page says it is not thought to be harmful to the baby, although the evidence is limited. For breastfeeding, one NHS page says it is acceptable if the baby is healthy, while the main page says it is not usually used.

faqs.q: What are the serious warning signs with amlodipine?
faqs.a: The NHS says to call 999 for sudden swelling of the lips, mouth, throat or tongue, difficulty breathing, or chest pain that does not stop after a few minutes. It lists severe stomach pain and yellowing of the skin or whites of the eyes as possible signs of pancreas or liver problems. The NHS says serious side effects are rare.
